The main issues I'm spotting: the message hierarchy is weak — user and assistant turns don't have enough visual distinction beyond alignment and background, and that "Correction not kept" line is ambiguous about who it's directed to and what it means. The timestamp "1m ago" is repeated and low-value, and the action row (thumbs, copy, time) floats without clear grouping. The "Worked 15s" affordance is subtle and easy to miss, yet it's a critical part of the agent transparency story. The right rail toggle exists but there's no indication of what it contains, and the overall layout wastes horizontal space with a fixed-width column that doesn't adapt well to the viewport.

The input row has some nice touches — the caret is visible and the mic button is clear — but the "Agents" chip above it is the only signal of worker activity, which feels thin for a multi-agent product. The tab bar shows project names but no status indicators for running agents or unread activity. The color palette is monochrome gray-on-black with low contrast for secondary text, and the system message "Correction not kept" is nearly invisible. There's no visual anchor like an avatar or colored marker to tell you who's speaking, and long prose blocks don't have a way to collapse or quote them. The version number and settings gear are tucked in the bottom-left, which is fine but easy to overlook.

I'm thinking about how to structure the feedback — maybe a prioritized list of the biggest wins, then a few smaller nits, and offer to write a design doc if they want something more durable.

Read the screenshot closely. The bones are good — calm dark theme, single reading column, "Worked 15s" disclosure, per-message actions. What I'd change, biggest first:

1. **Speaker anchoring.** Nothing in a reply says *who* is talking — no name, avatar, or color key. With agents, sub-agents, and kernel messages sharing one column, every turn starts by re-deriving who wrote it. A small identity mark per turn fixes that.

2. **The kernel line is cryptic.** "Correction not kept" with a loop glyph sits at the end of *my* message, styled like prose, and reads like part of the reply. System messages need their own visual class — different color, maybe a left rule — and human-readable text ("I saved the correction just now"), because right now it's a log entry leaking into the chat.

3. **The empty margins are the design's biggest untapped asset.** ~25% of the window on each side does nothing. That's exactly where a worker/plan rail belongs — live agent rows, the todo card — instead of a lone "Agents" chip floating above the input. The panel toggle at top-right hints one exists but nothing signals what it contains.

4. **Turn separation is weak.** "continue" as a floating pill and "Worked 15s" as a gray line are the only boundaries between long prose blocks; after three paragraphs the eye loses the turn structure. A faint divider or slightly stronger user-chip contrast would help.

5. **Tabs carry no state.** Three project tabs, all identical weight. A dot for "a worker is running here" or "unread reply" is the one thing that makes multi-project tabs worth having.

6. **Small stuff:** "1m ago" twice adds nothing — keep absolute time on hover only; secondary gray is below comfortable contrast; the prose column could be a touch wider (~80ch) before it hurts; the composer's caret blinking in "Send follow-up" makes the placeholder read as typed text.

If I had to ship one: #3 — the rail. It converts the layout's dead space into the product's actual differentiator (visible agents), and #1 and #2 get easier once there's a place to hang identity.

Thinking.text:
The user is asking for design feedback on their chat panel screenshot. I can see the layout with tabs at the top (`.arbos`, `Arena-GPS`, `testarbos` with a close button), a centered message column on a dark background, and a three-dot menu with what looks like a panel toggle in the top right.

Looking at the message flow, I notice the assistant's long prose response is followed by a "Correction not kept" system line that appears oddly placed — it's attached to the end of my previous message rather than clearly marked as system feedback. The user's "continue" message sits in a right-aligned pill, and below that is a "Worked 15s >" disclosure line showing my latest response with thumbs up/down, copy, and timestamp actions. At the bottom there's an "Agents" chip, an input field with a plus button and send control, a model selector showing "Qwen3.8 Flash," and a microphone option. The footer shows "This Mac" with a dropdown and version info "0.2.0 (1403)" with a gear icon.

The main issues I'm spotting: the message hierarchy is weak — user and assistant turns don't have enough visual distinction beyond alignment and background, and that "Correction not kept" line is ambiguous about who it's directed to and what it means. The timestamp "1m ago" is repeated and low-value, and the action row (thumbs, copy, time) floats without clear grouping. The "Worked 15s" affordance is subtle and easy to miss, yet it's a critical part of the agent transparency story. The right rail toggle exists but there's no indication of what it contains, and the overall layout wastes horizontal space with a fixed-width column that doesn't adapt well to the viewport.

The input row has some nice touches — the caret is visible and the mic button is clear — but the "Agents" chip above it is the only signal of worker activity, which feels thin for a multi-agent product. The tab bar shows project names but no status indicators for running agents or unread activity. The color palette is monochrome gray-on-black with low contrast for secondary text, and the system message "Correction not kept" is nearly invisible. There's no visual anchor like an avatar or colored marker to tell you who's speaking, and long prose blocks don't have a way to collapse or quote them. The version number and settings gear are tucked in the bottom-left, which is fine but easy to overlook.

I'm thinking about how to structure the feedback — maybe a prioritized list of the biggest wins, then a few smaller nits, and offer to write a design doc if they want something more durable.

items.Agent:
Read the screenshot closely. The bones are good — calm dark theme, single reading column, "Worked 15s" disclosure, per-message actions. What I'd change, biggest first:

1. **Speaker anchoring.** Nothing in a reply says *who* is talking — no name, avatar, or color key. With agents, sub-agents, and kernel messages sharing one column, every turn starts by re-deriving who wrote it. A small identity mark per turn fixes that.

2. **The kernel line is cryptic.** "Correction not kept" with a loop glyph sits at the end of *my* message, styled like prose, and reads like part of the reply. System messages need their own visual class — different color, maybe a left rule — and human-readable text ("I saved the correction just now"), because right now it's a log entry leaking into the chat.

3. **The empty margins are the design's biggest untapped asset.** ~25% of the window on each side does nothing. That's exactly where a worker/plan rail belongs — live agent rows, the todo card — instead of a lone "Agents" chip floating above the input. The panel toggle at top-right hints one exists but nothing signals what it contains.

4. **Turn separation is weak.** "continue" as a floating pill and "Worked 15s" as a gray line are the only boundaries between long prose blocks; after three paragraphs the eye loses the turn structure. A faint divider or slightly stronger user-chip contrast would help.

5. **Tabs carry no state.** Three project tabs, all identical weight. A dot for "a worker is running here" or "unread reply" is the one thing that makes multi-project tabs worth having.

6. **Small stuff:** "1m ago" twice adds nothing — keep absolute time on hover only; secondary gray is below comfortable contrast; the prose column could be a touch wider (~80ch) before it hurts; the composer's caret blinking in "Send follow-up" makes the placeholder read as typed text.

If I had to ship one: #3 — the rail. It converts the layout's dead space into the product's actual differentiator (visible agents), and #1 and #2 get easier once there's a place to hang identity.
